ORLANDO, Florida (CNN) -- The meter reader who led authorities last week to remains believed to be those of Caylee Anthony called police four months ago, directing them three times to same site, authorities said Thursday. Caylee Anthony, 2, has been missing since June in a case that has received national attention. At a news conference, Capt. Angelo Nieves, an Orange County Sheriff's Department commander, said investigators are looking into whether the tips, called in August 11, 12 and 13, were properly followed up. In one of those phone calls, the meter reader reported seeing a gray bag on the side of the road, Nieves said. On August 13, a deputy responded to the site and did a "cursory search" but found nothing, Nieves said. Casey Anthony, 22, faces charges including first-degree murder in the June disappearance of her daughter, Caylee, who was 2 at the time. Remains described as being those of a small child were found last week a half-mile from Casey Anthony's parents' home, in the area where the meter reader first directed police. Nieves said police were getting more information from the tipster and the deputy who responded to the tips. He said the department was investigating the "thoroughness" of the deputy's response but would not identify the deputy. The meter reader "is not a suspect," Nieves said. "He is a credible witness." Nieves' latest announcement is raising questions about whether police missed several chances to find remains believed to be Caylee's. The meter reader is not the only one, or the first, to have pointed police toward the site containing the remains. KioMarie Cruz, Casey Anthony's childhood friend, also told police to investigate the same wooded area near Hidden Oaks Elementary School a month before the meter reader, according to CNN affiliate WFTV. In an interview with detectives, according to WFTV, Cruz said that she and Anthony "pretty much used to hang out there most of our time," would "snack on food for hours" and went there to "get away from our parents." The sheriff's office followed up on that tip, but the wooded area was covered in floodwaters, preventing a search. Nieves said the water may have been present at the time of the meter reader's tips as well. Nieves also said Thursday that searchers combing the site after the skull's discovery had found "significant skeletal remains" consistent with those of a small child on the outer perimeter of the search area. The area will be enlarged, and processing and searching of the site will continue, probably into the weekend, he said. Some of the remains have been sent to the FBI lab in Quantico, Virginia, in an effort to identify them. Authorities have said the remains are believed to be Caylee's, but an identification is pending. Sheriff's spokesman Carlos Padilla said last week that authorities believe the remains are Caylee's for three reasons: No other children have been reported missing in the area; the remains are consistent with those of a child of Caylee's age; and the remains were found near the home of the grandparents, where the 2-year-old and her mother were living just before Caylee disappeared. FBI spokesman Richard Kolko said Monday that he did not know when tests would be complete, but an attorney for Anthony's parents said the FBI is likely to have results "within the next week." Casey Anthony could face a sentence of life in prison if convicted. Prosecutors said this month that they would not seek the death penalty.

Angelo Nieves said officials were reviewing how investigators handled tips received from the meter reader on August 11, 12 and 13. Caylee’s mother, 22-year-old Casey Anthony, has been charged with first-degree murder and other offenses in connection with her daughter’s disappearance. If found guilty, she could be sentenced to life in prison. Prosecutors announced this month that they would not pursue the death penalty.

Last week, remains described as those of a young child were discovered about half a mile from the home of Casey Anthony’s parents. The site was in the same area the meter reader had previously identified to law enforcement.

According to Nieves, investigators were seeking additional details from both the tipster and the deputy who responded. The department was examining whether the deputy’s actions were sufficiently thorough, he said, but officials declined to name the deputy.

Nieves emphasized that the meter reader was not under suspicion, describing him instead as a reliable witness.

The disclosure has prompted questions about whether authorities passed up multiple opportunities to locate the remains believed to be Caylee’s. The meter reader was neither the first nor the only person to direct police to the area where they were eventually found.

A month before his calls, KioMarie Cruz, a childhood friend of Casey Anthony, told detectives to examine the same wooded location near Hidden Oaks Elementary School, CNN affiliate WFTV reported.

According to WFTV’s account of her interview with investigators, Cruz said she and Anthony spent much of their time there when they were younger. She recalled that they would sit for hours eating snacks and used the place as a retreat from their parents.

The sheriff’s office acted on Cruz’s information, but flooding had submerged the woods and made a search impossible. Nieves said the location might also have remained underwater when the meter reader contacted police.

Nieves also reported Thursday that teams searching the property after a skull was found had recovered substantial skeletal material matching that of a small child along the search zone’s outer boundary. He said authorities planned to expand the perimeter and expected the examination and search of the site to continue, likely through the weekend.

Some of the recovered material was sent to the FBI laboratory in Quantico, Virginia, for identification. Although investigators have said they think the remains are Caylee’s, that conclusion had not yet been officially confirmed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about authorities investigating whether police mishandled three August tips from a meter reader who later discovered remains believed to be those of missing toddler Caylee Anthony.
counterfactuals.output:
# Authorities review handling of tips in Caylee Anthony case

**ORLANDO, Florida (CNN)** — Authorities are investigating whether deputies mishandled three August tips from a utility worker who later discovered remains believed to be those of missing Florida toddler Caylee Anthony.

Orange County officials said the meter reader contacted authorities on three consecutive days in August after noticing something suspicious in a wooded area near the Anthony family’s home. Deputies responded to the area, but no remains were found at the time.

Months later, the same worker returned to the location and discovered a small skull and other remains, prompting an extensive search by investigators. The site is less than half a mile from the home where Caylee lived with her mother and grandparents.

The Orange County Sheriff’s Office has launched an internal review to determine how the August calls were handled, whether deputies adequately searched the area and if department procedures were followed.

Investigators have not officially confirmed the identity of the remains, but authorities have said they believe they may belong to Caylee. Forensic specialists are examining the remains and evidence collected from the scene.

Caylee was 2 years old when she was last seen in June. Her disappearance was not reported to police until about a month later, when her grandmother called authorities.

The child’s mother, Casey Anthony, has been charged with murder and other offenses in connection with Caylee’s disappearance. She has pleaded not guilty and has maintained that she does not know what happened to her daughter.

The discovery has intensified scrutiny of the investigation, particularly the response to the meter reader’s earlier reports. Sheriff’s officials said the review would establish a timeline of the calls, identify the personnel involved and determine whether disciplinary action or changes in procedure are warranted.

Authorities continued searching the wooded area as they awaited forensic confirmation of the remains’ identity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the latest developments in the Caylee Anthony case, including the earlier reports about a gray bag, the deputy’s cursory search, KioMarie Cruz’s tip, and the FBI’s efforts to identify the remains.
counterfactuals.output:
- **Earlier “gray bag” reports:** In August 2008, Orange County utility worker **Roy Kronk** repeatedly called authorities about a suspicious object—described in some early reports as a gray or vinyl-looking bag—and what he believed might be a skull in woods near the Anthony family’s Orlando home. The area was swampy and heavily overgrown.

- **Deputy’s cursory search:** A deputy, **Richard Cain**, responded but conducted only a limited inspection from the roadside or edge of the flooded area and did not find or secure anything. Kronk returned in December, when water levels were lower, and discovered a child’s skull and a bag containing scattered remains. The sheriff’s office later acknowledged that the August response had been inadequate; Cain was disciplined and subsequently fired over his handling and reporting of the call.

- **KioMarie Cruz’s tip:** **KioMarie Cruz**, a former friend of Casey Anthony, told investigators that the wooded area near Hidden Oaks Elementary School was familiar to Casey and their friends and had been used as a hangout and a place where they had buried pets. Her information drew attention because the remains were ultimately found in that same general area, although it did not itself locate Caylee.

- **FBI identification work:** After the December 2008 discovery, the medical examiner and FBI examined the badly decomposed and scattered remains, using DNA testing, skeletal and hair analysis, and comparisons with Caylee’s family samples and known evidence. On **December 19, 2008**, authorities formally identified the remains as **2-year-old Caylee Anthony**.

The later legal outcome was that Casey Anthony was tried in 2011 and acquitted of murder, aggravated child abuse, and aggravated manslaughter, though she was convicted of providing false information to law enforcement. Caylee’s death remains officially classified as a homicide, but the precise cause and manner in which she died were never conclusively established.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

**BREAKING NEWS | December 12, 2008**

# Discovery of Child’s Remains Raises Questions About Earlier Searches Near Anthony Home

**ORLANDO, Fla.** — The discovery of a child’s skeletal remains less than half a mile from the home of George and Cindy Anthony has intensified scrutiny of whether authorities and volunteer search teams missed earlier opportunities to examine the wooded site.

An Orange County utility worker found the remains Thursday morning in a swampy area off Suburban Drive, near the east Orlando home where 2-year-old Caylee Anthony lived before she was reported missing in July. Investigators have not formally identified the remains, and authorities cautioned Friday that forensic testing will be required to determine the child’s identity.

The location and the presence of items associated with a young child, however, have led investigators to treat the discovery as potentially connected to the nationally watched Caylee Anthony case.

The central question now confronting law-enforcement officials is how the remains could have gone undetected for months in an area so close to the Anthony family’s house—and whether warnings about that same location received adequate attention.

## Utility worker had reported suspicious area before

The Orange County Sheriff’s Office confirmed that the utility worker who made Thursday’s discovery had contacted authorities several times in August about something suspicious in or near the wooded area.

The worker, identified in news reports as county meter reader Roy Kronk, called a sheriff’s tip line on August 11, 12 and 13. A deputy was dispatched after the calls, but no remains were found at that time.

Sheriff’s officials said they are reviewing recordings, dispatch records and the responding deputy’s actions. They have not yet offered a complete public account of what Kronk reported, how precisely he described the location or how extensively the site was inspected.

Those details are crucial. If Kronk directed authorities to the same spot where the remains were found Thursday, the August response could represent a significant missed opportunity. If his earlier reports concerned a broader or different area, the connection may be less direct.

Officials warned against reaching conclusions before the review is completed.

## Water may have obstructed earlier searches

The terrain itself may help explain why the remains were not discovered sooner. The site lies in dense woods and low-lying, swampy ground that was affected by heavy summer rain.

Search organizers have said portions of the area were covered by water when volunteers looked for Caylee earlier in the year. Flooding, thick vegetation and poor visibility could have concealed a small body or prevented searchers from safely reaching the exact location.

Texas EquuSearch, the volunteer organization that mounted large searches for Caylee, examined areas around the Anthony neighborhood during two deployments. Its founder, Tim Miller, said searchers had been in the general vicinity but that water conditions limited access to some sections.

That distinction—between searching the neighborhood and searching the precise recovery site—is likely to become a major point of inquiry.

Maps, volunteer logs and GPS records may help establish how close organized search teams came to the remains. Investigators will also need to determine whether the site changed as floodwaters receded, exposing objects that had previously been submerged or obscured.

## Proximity to the Anthony home draws attention

The remains were found only a short distance from the house where Caylee had lived with her mother, Casey Anthony, and her maternal grandparents.

That proximity has prompted renewed attention to the roads and wooded parcels surrounding the home. From the beginning of the case, investigators searched vehicles, residences and other locations connected to the family. Numerous volunteer searches also covered parts of Orange County.

Yet the discovery suggests that one of the most important locations may have been close by all along.

It is not yet clear when the remains were placed at the site, how long they had been there or whether they had been moved. The medical examiner’s office will attempt to answer those questions through examination of the bones, surrounding soil, vegetation and any associated objects.

Investigators erected a large perimeter Thursday and continued processing the scene Friday. They sifted through debris and removed potential evidence while shielding the area from cameras and onlookers.

## Identification could take time

Orange County officials said the remains appear to be those of a young child, but they have not publicly confirmed age, sex or identity.

Forensic specialists are expected to compare dental evidence and DNA with known samples from Caylee and members of her family. The condition of the remains could affect how quickly that work can be completed.

Authorities also have declined to provide a detailed description of items recovered nearby. News organizations have reported that an object resembling a small skull was found with material around it, but investigators have urged the public not to rely on fragmentary or unofficial accounts.

Until the medical examiner completes the identification, the remains cannot conclusively be described as Caylee’s.

## Casey Anthony remains jailed

Casey Anthony, 22, is being held without bond on a first-degree murder charge and related counts in her daughter’s disappearance. She has pleaded not guilty.

Prosecutors have alleged that Caylee died in June and that Anthony concealed the death. Anthony’s defense has maintained that she did not kill her daughter and has challenged the state’s evidence.

Caylee was last reported to have been seen in mid-June, but authorities were not notified that she was missing until July 15, after Cindy Anthony contacted emergency dispatchers. During the intervening month, Casey Anthony gave relatives and investigators accounts that were later shown to contain false information, including claims about a babysitter and her place of employment.

No finding at the Suburban Drive site has yet been presented in court, and investigators have not publicly said whether the discovery changes the charges already pending.

## Review likely to focus on three issues

The developing inquiry into the missed-search question is expected to center on:

1. **The August tip calls:** What Kronk reported, whether he gave an exact location and how the sheriff’s office classified and relayed the information.

2. **The deputy’s response:** Where the deputy went, how long the inspection lasted, whether the deputy entered the woods and what conditions existed at the time.

3. **Volunteer-search coverage:** Whether organized teams searched the precise recovery site or were prevented from doing so by standing water, vegetation or safety concerns.

Those questions do not by themselves establish negligence. Search operations routinely involve large areas, uncertain tips and difficult terrain. But the fact that the eventual discovery was made by a person who had previously contacted authorities about the area is certain to generate close examination.

Sheriff’s officials said the internal review would proceed alongside the criminal investigation.

For the Anthony family and the community, the immediate focus remains identification. George and Cindy Anthony have repeatedly said they believed Caylee was alive and had continued seeking information about her whereabouts.

The wooded area off Suburban Drive remained closed Friday as investigators searched for additional evidence—while officials faced mounting demands to explain whether the site had been brought to their attention four months earlier and, if so, why nothing was found.

**Remains Believed to Be Caylee Anthony Undergo Forensic Examination**

**ORLANDO, Fla.** — Investigators are conducting forensic tests on a child’s remains found near the home of missing Florida toddler Caylee Anthony, whose mother, Casey Anthony, has been charged with her murder.

A utility worker discovered the remains in a wooded area near the Anthony family’s Orlando home. Authorities said the remains appeared to be those of a young child, but cautioned that a positive identification would require further examination.

The Orange County medical examiner’s office is working to determine the child’s identity and cause of death. Investigators also are examining evidence recovered from the scene, with some material expected to be sent to federal laboratories for DNA and other forensic testing.

Caylee was 2 years old when she was last seen in June 2008. Her disappearance was not reported to police until about a month later. Casey Anthony was indicted in October on charges including first-degree murder, aggravated child abuse, aggravated manslaughter of a child and providing false information to law enforcement. She has pleaded not guilty.

Anthony told investigators that Caylee had disappeared while in the care of a babysitter, but police said they were unable to verify that account.

Prosecutors have said they will not seek the death penalty, meaning Anthony would face life imprisonment if convicted of first-degree murder. That decision could be revisited if new evidence changes the circumstances of the case.

Authorities said the forensic examination could take days or longer and declined to speculate publicly about whether the remains are Caylee’s pending scientific confirmation.
